paragraphs.en: Think about the first hour of your day. You probably brushed your teeth, made a drink and checked your phone without really deciding to do any of these things. Psychologists believe that a considerable part of everyday behaviour works in this way. Rather than being the result of careful choices, many of our actions are habits, performed almost automatically and often without our full awareness. This is not necessarily a bad thing.

Researchers often describe a habit as a loop made up of three parts. First comes a cue, a signal that triggers the behaviour, such as a particular time, place or feeling. Next is the routine, which is the behaviour itself. Finally, there is a reward, something pleasant that makes the brain more likely to repeat the loop. When a phone vibrates, for example, the sound acts as a cue, picking up the phone is the routine, and the small satisfaction of a new message is the reward.

Habits appear to form through repetition in a stable context. Each time a cue is followed by the same action and a reward, the connection between them grows stronger, until the behaviour requires very little conscious thought. This has a clear advantage, because it frees attention for other tasks. How long the process takes, however, is far from certain. The popular claim that any habit forms in exactly three weeks is probably an oversimplification, since the time seems to vary greatly between people and between behaviours.

Many people who want to change their lives rely on willpower. Unfortunately, self-control is not always dependable. Some psychologists have argued that it works like a limited resource which becomes weaker as the day goes on, although this idea remains controversial and later research has not always supported it. Whatever the explanation, people who seem highly disciplined often depend less on willpower than others imagine. Instead, they tend to organise their surroundings so that temptation rarely appears.

One practical strategy is known as habit stacking. Instead of trying to create a new habit from nothing, a person attaches it to something they already do every day. A simple plan might be: after I pour my morning tea, I will read one page of a book. Because the existing habit is already firmly established, it can serve as a reliable cue for the new behaviour. The more specific the plan, the easier it tends to be to follow.

Breaking a bad habit is often harder than starting a good one. Some experts recommend keeping the cue and the reward but changing the routine in between, for instance going for a short walk instead of reaching for a snack when feeling stressed. It also helps to make cues for unwanted habits less visible and to make good habits as easy as possible. Someone who wants to exercise in the morning might leave their sports clothes next to the bed the night before.

None of this means that change happens overnight. Building a habit is usually a slow process, and progress is rarely smooth. Encouragingly, missing a single day does not seem to undo the effort that has already been made. What matters most, it appears, is returning to the routine rather than giving up after one mistake. Small, realistic steps are generally more successful than dramatic promises.

Scientists now agree that willpower runs out like fuel during the day.

explain.uz: «First comes a cue, a signal that triggers the behaviour».

explain.uz: «they tend to organise their surroundings so that temptation rarely appears».
